content.title: Top 30 Irish films of all time: numbers 30-21 - featuring Belfast, Wolfwalkers and Sing Street
content.text: Here is the start of our list of the very best movies, as voted by 30 film-makers and critics What makes our favourite films our favourite films? Nostalgia? Beloved stars? Stunning cinematography? Heartrending scenes and gripping stories?It can be a subjective business, which is why we cast our net wide and deep for our selection of the 30 best Irish feature films. It was chosen by a distinguished panel of film-makers, producers, critics, broadcasters, programmers, distributors and festival directors who are well placed to assess the state of our national cinema. A list of more than 70 exceptional Irish films was whittled down to a final list of 30.Here is the top 30 to 21. Look out tomorrow for the countdown from 20 to 11.30. Hush-a-bye-Baby (1989) As raw and powerful as the day it was released, Margo Harkin’s unflinching and insightful drama follows the fortunes of Goretti (Emer McCourt), a teenage Derry girl who is involved in a tentative relationship with Ciarán, an Irish speaker and ardent republican. When he is arrested for suspected membership of the IRA, Goretti begins to feel ill and realises to her horror that she is pregnant. Overcome with terror, she hides her condition from her family and her best friends Dinky, Sinéad and Majella and removes herself to the Donegal Gaeltacht to improve her Irish. Ciarán, she reckons, will understand, but when she finally tells him, he reacts with cruel indifference, leading Goretti to consider desperate measures. McCourt is superb in the leading role, and Sinéad O’Connor is a wonderfully ethereal presence as Goretti’s friend Sinéad. A powerful film, and a brave one, especially for its time.29. Wolfwalkers (2020) The hardest thing for Kilkenny animation titans Cartoon Saloon must be matching their own high standards, but in Wolfwalkers they managed to surpass them. More ambitious visually than previous films including The Secret of Kells and Song of the Sea, Wolfwalkers is set in 17th century Ireland, where England’s invading Lord Protector has established himself in a walled town. Wolves lurk in the forests around, and Cromwell has brought a master hunter called Bill Goodfellowe (voiced by Sean Bean) to wipe them out. As a result, Goodfellowe’s daughter Robyn (Honor Kneafsey) is left to her own devices, and one day she gets lost in the forest and meets a strange girl called Mebh (Eva Whittaker). She is a Wolfwalker, an ancient tribe said to commune with wolves and transform into them at night, and soon Robyn is caught between two very different worlds. The film’s animation is gorgeous, cleverly contrasting the boxy lines of the walled town with the vibrant wildness of the wilderness the invader is so keen to expunge.Caitriona Balfe, Jamie Dornan, Judi Dench, Jude Hill and Lewis McAskie in the film Belfast28. Belfast (2021) Kenneth Branagh is perhaps the plummiest Shakespearean actor of his generation, but once he spoke with a very different voice. Born in Belfast in 1960, he left the city at the age of nine as a consequence of the Troubles, which devastated the working-class Protestant enclave from which his family hailed. In this sumptuous drama, filmed mainly in crisp black and white, Branagh evokes the fleeting intimacy of his Northern Irish childhood, which is about to be shattered by riots, bombs and cross-community gangsterism. Buddy (the excellent Jude Hill) is a bright and lively nine-year-old who lives with his parents (Jamie Dornan and Caitríona Balfe) and older brother in the cramped but cosy working-class streets of north Belfast. Civil rights marches, and the furious response of the Orange state, have led to wide unrest. The onset of the Troubles leads his family to make a fateful and difficult decision. Ciarán Hinds and Judi Dench play Buddy’s doting grandparents in this irresistible and heartfelt film.Read more27. Intermission (2003) “A likeable film about nasty people” was how American critic Richard Roeper described Intermission, and that pretty much sums it up. And while it was accused in its day of being sub-Tarantino, John Crowley and Mark O’Rowe’s swaggering comic crime caper is much more original than that. In one of Irish cinema’s most memorable openings, petty thief Lehiff (Colin Farrell) flirts with a young shop cashier (Kerry Condon), then punches her in the face and robs the till. Lehiff is high on the hit list of Jerry Lynch (Colm Meaney) a deeply unpleasant garda detective who believes it is his divine mission to drive the “scumbags” off Dublin’s streets. A galaxy of supporting characters includes warring couple John and Deirdre (Cillian Murphy and Kelly Macdonald), luckless Romeo Oscar (David Wilmot), and an odious small boy with a talent for causing chaos. Intermission is of its time perhaps, but full of memorable moments.26. Maeve (1981) Pat Murphy’s remarkable 1980s drama managed to be both dreamlike and sternly realistic at once. Shot on the fly on the streets of Belfast, it tells the story of Maeve Sweeney (Mary Jackson), a young woman from a nationalist background who returns to Northern Ireland after studying in London just as the Troubles reach their height. As she reckons with her past, she feels alienated by everything around her, from the RUC who once beat her to the arrogant, swaggering British soldiers to the sexist dogmatism of the IRA. Her boyfriend Liam (John Keegan) is a member, and haughtily explains that “I represent the women here more than you do”. Bríd Brennan plays her sister Róisín, and Murphy’s brilliant feature moves fluently back and forth in time to give us a fuller picture of Maeve’s turbulent life.‘Superb central performances from Donal McCann, Ciarán Hinds and Saskia Reeves capture a sparse, Bible-bound Ulster. Director Thaddeus O’Sullivan throws light into dark corners’ Seán Rocks on December BrideCiarán Hinds and Saskia Reeves in December Bride25. December Bride (1990) A boldly original Irish film based on a novel by northern novelist Sam Hanna Bell, Thaddeus O’Sullivan’s stately and absorbing drama stars Saskia Reeves as Sarah Gilmartin, a single-minded young woman whose contempt for convention causes ructions in a small Ulster town. It’s 1909, and Sarah arrives with her mother to work as housekeeper for a widower and his two grown sons. Scandalised by the family’s laissez-faire attitude to church-going, the mother quickly departs, but Sarah settles right in, and begins a relationship with the younger brother Frank (Ciarán Hinds). Before you know it, older brother Hamilton (Donal McCann) has joined in, and when Sarah falls pregnant, she refuses to marry either sibling or reveal who the father is. She emerges as something of a counterculture heroine in this thought-provoking drama.Jack Reynor and Ferdia Walsh-Peelo in Sing Street24. Sing Street (2016) John Carney has made a number of fine films, but while Once might be the best known, Sing Street is more substantial and likeable. Loosely based on Carney’s youth, the musical drama follows the fortunes of Conor Lalor (Ferdia Walsh-Peelo), who is not best pleased when his father pulls him out of an exclusive private school and sends him to Synge Street, the inner-city Christian Brothers’ school. Conor thinks it’s the end of the world but in fact it’s a new beginning, as he joins forces with like-minded teens to form a band. It’s all being done to impress a girl of course, the grand and ethereal Raphina (Lucy Boynton), who claims she’s a model and plans to move to London. Don Wycherley gives an amusing turn as an apoplectic Christian Brother and Jack Reynor is very good as Conor’s laconic, pot-smoking older brother. All in all, a heartwarming film.23. His & Hers (2009) In his debut feature, Portarlington film-maker Ken Wardrop made good on the promise of his short documentaries with an absorbing exploration of Irish womanhood. Filming with a small crew in the heart of the midlands, he asks females from the age of five or six to 90 to discuss the men in their lives, from brothers and fathers to husbands and sons. His & Hers builds an extraordinary cumulative power that reaches its climax in the recollections of elderly ladies including Wardrop’s own mother about coping with the death of the men they loved. Wardrop shoots all of this simply and directly, with a fixed camera: the faces and the personalities provide the fireworks, though he often situates his subjects near homely props that give hints as to their deeper stories. Funny, profound and lovely to look at, Wardrop’s film presents an intriguing kaleidoscope of the Irish female experience.‘This stunning work from Pat Murphy is a historical reclamation of the story of Robert Emmett’s so-called housekeeper, Anne Devlin. Based intensely on Anne’s prison writing, it’s beautifully shot, with that famous tableau of the noble Bríd Brennan standing up in a horse and cart as she’s surrounded by redcoats’ Margo Harkin on Anne Devlin22. Anne Devlin (1984) The second Pat Murphy film to make our list, this eloquent historical drama tells the story of Anne Devlin, who conspired with Robert Emmett to overthrow British rule in Ireland. Incensed by the brutal repression of the 1798 rising, Anne (Bríd Brennan) becomes an active insurrectionist, and introduces Emmett to her Wicklow cousin Michael Dwyer, who promises to lead a rebellion from the mountains if Emmett can supply him with guns. While posing as Emmett’s housekeeper, Anne conspired in the planning of the 1803 rebellion, which failed miserably but would become a beacon of hope for republicans. Making a film in Ireland in the mid-1980s was no joke, but with Thaddeus O’Sullivan as her cinematographer, Murphy managed to make something pretty special. “With Anne Devlin’s journal,” she said afterwards, “I wanted to tell a story that was like a ballad.” She did just that.Richard Dormer (centre) as Terri in Good Vibrations21. Good Vibrations (2012) Lisa Barros D’Sa’s wryly amusing drama is set in Northern Ireland at the start of the Troubles and tells the rousing tale of Terri Hooley. A music-obsessed hippie, Terri (Richard Dormer) decides to open a record shop in downtown Belfast at a time when retailers were deserting it in droves. In the film’s most pivotal scene, Terri has a eureka moment after stumbling into a raucous gig by a young punk outfit called the Outcasts. Gripped by one of his characteristic enthusiasms, he sets up a record label to promote singles by bands such as the Outcasts and Rudi, and then one day, the Undertones walk into his shop and present him with a demo. Good Vibrations brilliantly evokes the edgy paranoia of ’70s Belfast, and gives a sense of what was going on in the background without getting bogged down in history. And Dormer is exceptionally good as the charming and eternally optimistic Hooley.Tomorrow on Independent.ie: the top 30 Irish films, numbers 20-11The judgesRuth Barton (professor in Film Studies, TCD); Sarina Bellissimo (critic); Frank Berry (film-maker); Declan Burke (critic, The Examiner); Fiona Clark (director, Cork Film Festival); Nick Costello (GM, Universal Picture Int, Ireland); Kevin Coyne (programmer, IFI); Lance Daly (film-maker); Michael Doherty (critic, RTÉ Guide); Sinéad Egan (producer, Arena); Siobhán Farrell (film publicist); Kathryn Ferguson (film-maker and curator); Will Fitzgerald (film programmer, Light House/Palás); Alan Gilsenan (film-maker); Glenn Hogarty (industry publicist); Margo Harkin (film-maker); Grainne Humphreys (Director, Dublin Film Festival); John Kelleher (film & TV producer, former censor); Cara O’Doherty (critic, The Echo); David O Mahony (Head of programming, IFI); Esther McCarthy (critic, Sunday World); Maeve McGrath (Director, Galway Film Fleadh); Deirdre Molumby (film writer, independent.ie); Seán Munsanje (critic); Emer Reynolds (film-maker); Seán Rocks (presenter, Arena); Rob Walpole (film producer); Dearbhla Walsh (film-maker); Chris Wasser (critic, Sunday Independent); Hilary A White (critic, Sunday Independent) Read more
